newsitem.title: UK: New Israeli settlements may hurt peace process - UK.
newsitem.headline: New Israeli settlements may hurt peace process - UK.

text.p: Britain said on Wednesday the creation of new Israeli settlements might disrupt the Middle East peace process and it urged speedy negotiations to avert possible confrontation.
"New settlements cannot help the peace process," Jeremy Hanley, a junior Foreign Office minister, said after talks with the speaker of the Palestinian Legislative Council, Ahmed Qurie.
"These possible actions should be avoided and we hope that they will be, and that the parties continue their search for peace," he told reporters.
"Talk together...and the quicker, of course, the better."
Qurie was in London for three days of official talks on issues ranging from the Middle East peace talks to Britain's parliamentary process and aid for the Palestinian people.
He said his "fruitful talks" with Hanley came at a critical period, with tensions heightened by the settlement question.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pledged on Wednesday to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem over Palestinian objections.

Critics said the plan would spark Palestinian rage that could prove more costly than gun battles in which 61 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers died last year after Netanyahu opened a new entrance to a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.

The PLO wants Arab East Jerusalem, captured by Israel along with the rest of the West Bank in 1967, to be the capital of a future Palestinian( state and has called Israeli housing projects an attempt to cement the Jewish state's hold over all of the city. Israel views all of Jerusalem as its capital.
Hanley said the European Union disagreed.
"The future of Jerusalem should be determined by peaceful means. Actions which pre-empt the final status of Jerusalem are undesirable and do not help the search for peace," he said.
Although Israel has handed to Palestinian self-rule some areas of the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip, the status of Jerusalem is not due to be decided for a few years.
Hanley also discussed Palestinian human rights abuses with Qurie, saying: "We recognise that breaches of human rights are regrettable and should be avoided by both parties."

As for reports that some non-governmental organisations are angered by their treatment under Palestinian rule, Qurie said new laws were under discussion to support their work and expressed confidence "past misunderstandings" would be resolved very quickly.
